clue.text: The value of heating — or eating?

definitions.text: The value of heating — or eating?

parts.words: The value of heating — or eating?
parts.note: the heat a fuel gives out has a technical name used by engineers, and the same adjective describes rich, fattening food

explanation.surface: A question about what warmth, or a meal, is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: Engineers speak of the 'calorific value' of a fuel; the question mark adds the dieter's sense of food full of calories.
explanation.definitionFit: Calorific means relating to heat production, as in a fuel's heating value, and also describes fattening food.

parts.note: not dull people with blocky features but solids each bounded by six equal squares

explanation.surface: People with blocky, unattractive features.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular solid with six identical square sides, like dice or sugar lumps.

parts.note: 4 down means informal or costing nothing; time described that way is the hours away from work

explanation.surface: A musical time signature.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' stands for the answer to 4 down, FREE AND EASY; free time is spare time, away from work.
explanation.definitionFit: Free time is time away from work or duties, one's spare hours.

clue.text: It would be too heavy for the angler as a rule

definitions.text: It would be too heavy for the angler as a rule

parts.words: It would be too heavy for the angler as a rule
parts.note: a metal fishing pole would be far too weighty, and 'rule' points to the idiom for harsh, strict government

explanation.surface: Normally, this would weigh too much for a fisherman to carry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a rule' seems to mean 'usually', but the answer is a phrase for tyrannical rule; read literally it is a metal pole, too heavy for fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule with a rod of iron is to govern harshly; literally it is an iron bar, unlike a light fishing rod.

definitions.meaning: costing nothing and posing no hardship

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a relaxed, casual manner; split up, it means costing nothing and causing no trouble.

clue.text: Beast that grows a crest in' a Roman cemetery

indicators.note: the animal is what is left when a piece is removed, so adding it back grows the longer word

parts.note: the catacombs were the underground burial places of ancient Rome
a comb is the fleshy crest on a cockerel's head

explanation.surface: A creature that develops a crest in an ancient burial ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards: the beast plus A COMB (a crest) makes CATACOMB, the Roman underground cemetery, so taking A COMB away leaves the beast.
explanation.definitionFit: A feline animal, domestic or wild, counts as a beast.

parts.note: quel is the French word for what
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: Asking what a student of French is able to master.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' is a link word; 'overcome' is a verb here, not part of the student's achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: To quell a rebellion or a fear is to subdue and overpower it.

clue.text: In Ecuador, the 'place for leave, love

parts.note: to quit a place is to leave it
love is nil in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: Someone in Ecuador choosing between leaving and staying for love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the place' in Ecuador is its capital city; 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Quito is Ecuador's capital, the principal city of that country.

definitions.meaning: in the Bible the prophet Nathan's parable likens Bathsheba, taken by King David, to a poor man's single young female sheep
a person's most treasured possession, from the same parable

explanation.definitionFit: In Nathan's parable Bathsheba is a poor man's only young female sheep; the phrase has come to mean one's dearest treasure.

definitions.meaning: a secure position won, especially by troops in enemy ground
a deposit of money placed with a bank or fund

explanation.definitionFit: Military usage calls a captured position held as a base by this name; banking uses it for money paid in.

clue.text: Fifty, inbred originally, turn out streaky

indicators.note: the letters must turn out differently, a sign that they are rearranged

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Fifty animals, bred from close relatives, end up with streaked coats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn out' rearranges L (fifty) with INBRED to give BRINDLE; 'originally' just says these are the starting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Brindle describes a coat marked with darker streaks or tabby patches, as on some dogs and cattle.

parts.note: docking an animal means cutting short its tail, so the last part of it is what goes; the courtroom dock is the decoy

explanation.surface: A defendant's last hope vanishes in the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dock' suggests the prisoner's box, but docking is cutting off an animal's tail, and the hyphenated answer also means the final part of anything.
explanation.definitionFit: The tail-end is the very last part of something, and literally the end of the tail removed in docking.

parts.note: woollen cloth for uniforms, and also what a hungry army might be filled with

explanation.surface: Cloth fit to make soldiers' uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is old-fashioned for woven woollen cloth; as a verb it means to cram or overfeed, as one might the troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuff is a traditional name for woven fabric, especially woollen cloth.

definitions.meaning: a place where a ship lies at anchor
the largest city of the US state

explanation.definitionFit: A berth where vessels drop anchor; also the name of Alaska's biggest city.

clue.text: Anodyne, say, for one brought to bed

indicators.note: say signals that we only hear the words and spell them differently

parts.note: an anodyne is a painkiller, something to counter pain

explanation.surface: A painkiller, for instance, given to a woman in labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought to bed' is an old phrase for giving birth, but here it simply means carried to a bed: a bedspread. 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterpane is a bedspread, a cover laid on a bed.

parts.note: not a wonderful experience, as the idiom suggests, but how long one has lived

explanation.surface: Having a wonderful experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The time of one's life' is an idiom for a great experience, but read literally it is how old someone is.
explanation.definitionFit: How long a person has lived is their years, a span counted from birth.

clue.text: Grant one no turn on the instrument

parts.note: to accord something is to grant it
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: turn means the little word no is reversed

explanation.surface: Someone refusing to allow a single change in how a musical instrument is played.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses NO to ON; 'on the' then links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A portable keyboard bellows instrument, the squeezebox.

parts.note: a redoubt is a small fortification, a military earthwork
able means capable of being, so it stands for can be

explanation.surface: A fortification may be a daunting obstacle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something formidable inspires fear or respect through its power, exactly as a fearsome opponent does.

parts.note: a jack tar is a sailor, so jack gives TAR
taken as written, the man's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people, Jack and Paul, wearing nautical caps.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a sailor's waterproof hat of tarred cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin was a sailor's broad tarred hat, hence also a nickname for seamen.

clue.text: Shrub for the festival at Brooke's scene of nameless crimes

indicators.note: one piece is placed at the other, so the festival follows the village

parts.note: Rupert Brooke's poem Grantchester says 'Coton's full of nameless crimes', Coton being a village near Cambridge
Easter is the Christian spring festival

explanation.surface: A bush planted for a holiday at a notorious spot in a poet's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke's poem 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester' mocks the villages near Cambridge, including Coton, 'full of nameless crimes'. 'at' places EASTER after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cotoneaster is a genus of shrubs with small leaves and red berries, widely planted in gardens.

clue.text: Nominal trial arranged to include address familiar to Frenchmen.

indicators.note: include means the rearranged word holds the other piece within it
arranged means the letters of trial are put in a new order

parts.note: tu is the informal French word for you

explanation.surface: A token court case set up to involve informal French speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' turns TRIAL into TILAR; 'to include' puts TU inside it after TI.
explanation.definitionFit: Titular means in name only, holding a title without real power.

definitions.meaning: to shoot at, as in a snooker or game shot
slang for cannabis, the drug made from the hemp plant

explanation.definitionFit: To pot is to shoot game or sink a ball; as slang it is marijuana, a drug from Indian hemp.

clue.text: Guinea-fowl gets milk all the same

parts.note: a pinta is British slang for a pint of milk, from an old advertising slogan
do, short for ditto, means the same again

explanation.surface: A bird is given milk just like the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' is a link word. PINTA is British for a pint of milk; DO is ditto.
explanation.definitionFit: Pintado is a name for the guinea fowl, from the Portuguese for painted, after its spotted plumage.

parts.note: a property occupier who pays the local tax set at a fixed charge per property

explanation.surface: A homeowner who keeps to the published charges.
explanation.walkthrough: Before council tax, British householders paid 'rates', a local property tax; the tariff is the rate they pay.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a householder paid local rates on property, so was called by the name of one who pays them.

definitions.meaning: an independent school in Cambridge, England
the Latin phrase ..., by itself or in essence

explanation.definitionFit: The Perse School is a Cambridge school; written as two words, the Latin per se means in itself.

clue.text: She sang the final note badly.

indicators.note: singing badly suggests the letters come out wrong, so they are rearranged
only the final letter of the word note is used

explanation.surface: A woman sang the last note of a song out of tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the final' takes E, the end of 'note'; 'badly' mixes it with SANG.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, so it can stand for any woman referred to as she.

parts.note: found by looking, which is sighted, and the ear hears that word as one meaning placed

explanation.surface: Something tracked down using sight and hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Located' is the meaning; 'by eye' suggests a word for seen, and 'ear' says it sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sited means placed or situated in a particular location.

parts.note: rude in behaviour, and literally of poor breeding like a dog of mixed parentage

explanation.surface: A comparison of someone's rudeness to a scruffy dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated word means both rude and, literally, badly bred, as a mongrel is.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-bred means rude through poor upbringing, and also of inferior breeding, as with a crossbred dog.

definitions.meaning: an excavation of an ancient site

explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses it for liking or understanding; archaeologists use it for an excavation.

clue.text: In any event 'salt with tea is eccentric .

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and irregular, so the letters are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Putting salt in your tea is odd, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the two words of fodder; 'is eccentric' rearranges SALT and TEA.
explanation.definitionFit: At least, like 'in any event', means whatever else is true, anyway.

parts.note: not a girl raised in a foster family, but a senior hospital worker, called sister, who fosters patients' health

explanation.surface: A girl brought up in the same foster home.
explanation.walkthrough: A senior hospital ward nurse is called a sister in Britain, and to nurse a patient is to foster them back to health.
explanation.definitionFit: A ward sister is a senior hospital carer, and caring for the sick fosters their recovery.

parts.note: a reference to the title of a Thomas Hardy novel naming a tree, Under the ... Tree

explanation.surface: A tree tough enough to survive frost, at least in name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hardy' looks like a description of a tough tree but points to Thomas Hardy's novel 'Under the Greenwood Tree'.
explanation.definitionFit: A forest or woodland in leaf is the old poetic term used in the title of Thomas Hardy's novel.
